C-JXE-001.title_en: "Horizontal Transplantation" — Cross-Cultural Borrowing in Taiwan's Modern Poetry Movement
C-JXE-001.description_en: In the 1950s, Ji Xian proposed his 'horizontal transplantation' theory in Taiwan's poetry scene, advocating direct learning from Western modernist poets (Baudelaire, Rimbaud, Eliot) rather than following the longitudinal lineage of traditional Chinese poetics. This concept, promoted through his Modern Poetry quarterly, fundamentally changed the direction of Taiwanese poetry and became a milestone in the history of Chinese-language modern poetry.

C-JXE-002.title_en: "Emphasis on Intellectuality" — The Dominant Role of Rational Reflection in Poetry Creation
C-JXE-002.description_en: Ji Xian explicitly stated in his six commandments that 'new poetry is the emphasis on intellectuality,' arguing that poetry should not rely solely on emotional lyricism but should incorporate rational reflection and intellectual thought. This is embodied in works like 'Your Name,' where gentle language conceals philosophical depth about existence, memory, and emotional resonance.

C-JXE-003.title_en: "Pure Poetry" — Ontological Distinction Between Poetry and Prose
C-JXE-003.description_en: Ji Xian asserted that 'modern poetry is pure poetry, distinct from prose-poetry,' emphasizing poetry's independent ontological value and aesthetic autonomy. This theoretical stance liberated Taiwanese modern poetry from traditional lyricism, shifting toward pure exploration of language, form, and imagery, influencing subsequent generations of Taiwanese poets.

C-JXE-004.title_en: Existentialist Poetics — Philosophical Resources in Modern Poetry
C-JXE-004.description_en: Ji Xian argued that existentialism is a crucial source of modern poetry, introducing Sartre and Camus's philosophical ideas into poetic creation. His poems often use the 'lone wolf' metaphor, expressing individual loneliness, freedom, and resistance — transforming existentialist reflections on the human condition into profound poetic expression.

C-JXE-005.title_en: "Poetry as Humanity's Elevated Part" — Theoretical Construction of Poetry's Transcendent Value
C-JXE-005.description_en: In his six commandments, Ji Xian proposed that 'poetry is the elevated part of human life,' asserting that poetry should transcend everyday experience and reach spiritual elevation. This theory established a lofty value position for Taiwanese modern poetry, making poetry the vehicle of human spiritual freedom.

C-JXE-006.title_en: "Six Commandments" — Systematic Construction of Modern Poetic Theory
C-JXE-006.description_en: Ji Xian systematically proposed six commandments in Modern Poetry: horizontal transplantation, emphasis on intellectuality, pure poetry, existentialist source, elevated part, and new humanity. These six commandments formed a complete modern poetic theory system — from methodology (horizontal transplantation) to ontology (pure poetry) and axiology (elevated part) — providing a systematic theoretical framework for Taiwanese modern poetry.

C-JXE-007.title_en: "Lone Wolf" Spirit — The Artistic Persona of Solitary Independence
C-JXE-007.description_en: Ji Xian frequently identified himself as a 'lone wolf' in his poems, expressing an artistic persona that refused to conform and stood independent of crowds. Rejecting group-style creative models, he insisted on individual perspective and unique expression. This 'lone wolf' spirit became a spiritual symbol of Taiwan's modern poetry scene, influencing countless young poets pursuing artistic independence.

C-JXE-008.title_en: Blue Star Debate — Modern Poetry Route Controversy Case
C-JXE-008.description_en: Ji Xian's debates with the Blue Star Poetry Society (Qin Zihao, Yu Guangzhong et al.) were pivotal events in Taiwan's modern poetry history. Blue Star advocated 'lyrical tradition' and 'national spirit,' opposing Ji's 'horizontal transplantation.' This debate promoted Taiwan modern poetry's多元化 (diversity), deepening poetic creation through clashing philosophies.

C-JXE-009.title_en: "New Humanity" — Poetry's Value Orientation Toward Modern People
C-JXE-009.description_en: In his sixth commandment, Ji Xian declared that 'new poetry must belong to new humanity (modern humans),' advocating that poetry should address modern society's people and their existential circumstances. This shifted Taiwanese modern poetry from classical lyricism toward attention to modern humans' spiritual conditions, infusing poetry with contemporary relevance and realistic concern.

C-JXE-010.title_en: Lifelong Creative Practice — Validating Poetic Theory Through Continuous Creation
C-JXE-010.description_en: From his active years in 1930s Shanghai literary circles, to founding Modern Poetry quarterly in Taiwan (1953), and continuing creative output into old age (including 'Fifty at Ninety' published at age 90), Ji Xian validated his poetic theory through nearly a century of continuous creative practice. Even at 90, he maintained active thinking and rich imagination — 'still very beautiful' — setting an example of lifelong creative dedication.
